1                                               I.THE PARTIES
2
                     1.Plaintiff Claude B. Hutchison is a resident of the State of Nevada, and, for
3
     diversity jurisdictional purposes, a ‘citizen’ thereof and the owner of real property in the County
4
     of Monterey, California, for which he bought a policy of home warranty insurance from
5

6    Defendants. He is over 70 years of age. Having had an illustrious career including government

7    service in Washington D.C., and as a Regent of the University of California, Plaintiff is highly
8
     qualified to represent this class.
9
         1. Plaintiff class is that group of individuals over 70 years of age resident in all
10
     states wherein defendants do business (other than the State of New Jersey) who purchased
11

12   policies of home warranty insurance from Defendants and who had warranty claims denied,

13   delayed, or underpaid by Defendants. This is a class of defendants particularly vulnerable
14
     to the predations of Defendants.
15
         2. Defendant CHW Group, Inc., (hereinafter CHW) is a New Jersey corporation doing
16
     business as ‘Choice Home Warranty’ nationwide, including within the State of California.
17

18   It offers so called ‘home warranty protection’ insurance to homeowners in exchange for

19   premiums.
20
         3.Individual defendants Victor Hakim, Victor Mandalawi, David Seruya, and Maria
21
     Ramirez are owners, officers and/or directors of CHW. The individual defendants are all
22
     residents of New Jersey. The individual defendants are the alter egos of CHW, in that CHW
23

24   has no corporate identify separate from that of the individual defendants, and they use the

25   corporate fiction to mask their illegal activities and as a shield from liability.
26
        4. Plaintiff does not know the identifies of Doe Defendants I through 10 or Black and
27
     White Corporations 1-10 but believes that there are other individuals and corporations
28   COMPLAINT                                          2
                Case 5:24-cv-04876-VKD Document 1 Filed 08/08/24 Page 3 of 12



1    legally responsible for the damages sustained by Plaintiff and the Class, and begs leave
2
     to amend this pleading to include them when they have been identified through discovery.
3
     All the corporate, individual, and Doe defendants will be referred to, hereinafter, as
4
     “Defendants”.
5

6                                      II. JURISDICTION AND VENUE

7      5. This Court has jurisdiction over this class action by virtue of 28 U.S.C. 1332 (a) 1.
8
     Plaintiff’s ‘citizenship’- and causes of action on behalf of the class - satisfy the requirements of
9
     ‘minimal’ diversity. In an abundance of caution Plaintiff does not purport to represent
10
     class members who are citizens of New Jersey in order to achieve complete diversity.
11

12   Venue is in this district by virtue of 28 U.S.C. 1931 (b) (2) in so far as Plaintiff’s property

13   is located in Monterey County, California, and a substantial portion of the wrongs alleged
14
     occurred in Monterey County, California. Specifically, the claims occurred in territory
15
     serviced by the San Jose Division of this Court. The jurisdictional amount in controversy of
16
     $75,000.00 (Seventy-five thousand dollars) of this court is exceeded by plaintiff’s special,
17

18   compensatory, and punitive damages. Should the class of elderly victims of Defendants be

19   certified, their accumulated damages exceeds many millions of dollars. Plaintiff will comply
20
     specifically with Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 23 in a timely and appropriate manner.
21
                                       III. PLAINTIFF’S CLAIMS
22
                                     A. BREACH OF CONTRACT
23

24    6. Plaintiff entered into a written contract with Defendants whereby Defendants, in return for

25   payment of a substantial premium, promised to indemnity him for loss/damage to/ and wear
26
     of certain appliances in his Carmel Valley, California home, including an electric range. Plaintiff
27
     paid fora multi-year contract of appliance protection for two properties, including the Carmel
28   COMPLAINT                                         3
               Case 5:24-cv-04876-VKD Document 1 Filed 08/08/24 Page 4 of 12



1    Valley, California home. Within the last 12 (twelve) months immediately preceding the filing of
2
     this complaint, an electric range failed. Defendants sent a licensed contractor to examine the
3
     range, who made a determination that the range needed replacement. The replacement cost of the
4
     range, in so far as the model insured was no longer made, and due to the size constraints of the
5

6    kitchen, was approximately $9,000.00 (Nine thousand dollars)

7      7. Plaintiff performed his duties under Defendants policy of insurance, including payment of
8
     premium, reporting the loss, and cooperating with Defendants repair/replacement professional
9
     who made the assessment set forth in 6, supra.
10
       8. Defendants breached their obligations under the contract of insurance by:
11

12          a. Intentionally low-balling their offer of indemnity at $300.00 (Three hundred dollars)

13   without providing justification for such an offer. The offer was unreasonable, per se.
14
     This is a pattern and practice engaged in by Defendants nationwide. A relatively recent incident
15
     involving seniors can be viewed at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N6ntBiaNkxg which
16
     demonstrates that the pattern of ‘low-balling’ claimants is nationwide and directed primarily, it
17

18   would appear, at seniors who are a vulnerable class.

19          b. Intentionally delaying payment
20
            c. Creating untenable excuses for non-payment and unrealistic recovery limits.
21
            d. Failing to respond to Plaintiff’s communication demanding payment
22
            e. Failing to pay anything to Plaintiff
23

24          f. Causing plaintiff extreme emotional suffering in so far as his wife of 60 (sixty years)

25          passed away as this dispute was going on, in the Carmel Valley Home, at a time where
26
            there was no range available in the kitchen, specifically on May 4th, 2024, the date of
27
            Mrs. Hutchison’s death.
28   COMPLAINT                                        4
                Case 5:24-cv-04876-VKD Document 1 Filed 08/08/24 Page 5 of 12



1       9. As a proximate result of said breach, Plaintiff and the representative class have sustained
2
     special damages, compensatory damages, attorney’s fees and costs. Plaintiff additionally
3
     requests an award of punitive damages pursuant to California Civil Code 3294, in so far as
4
     Defendants have been guilty of fraud, oppression, and malice. Defendants scheme to defraud
5

6    potential insureds, particularly, elderly insureds, has been in existence for over a decade, and

7    specifically proven by the work of two State Attorney Generals, specifically, by the Attorney
8
     General of the State of New Jersey, CHW’s home state, in Attorney General of the State of New
9
     Jersey v. CHW Group Inc., C -135 -14 (2016) (hereinafter ‘New Jersey Regulatory Suit’ or
10
     NJRS) and by the Attorney General of the State of Arizona in State of Arizona v. CHW Group
11

12   Inc., CV -2019-013111 (2019) (hereinafter the Arizona Regulatory Suit or AZRS)

13                  A. RESCISSION PURSUANT TO CALIFORNIA CIVIL CODE 1689
14
        10. Plaintiff reincorporates and reallege allegations 1 through 9 as though fully set forth
15
     herein.
16
        11. Plaintiff’s consent to enter into the contract of home warranty insurance was induced
17

18   by fraud, specifically, Defendants intended to low-ball any claims made by Plaintiff under his

19   home warranty to ensure that the amount of premiums he paid always exceeded any amount
20
     of money they would owe him for appliances in need of replacement/repair under the policy
21
     in violation. See, California Civil Code 1689 (1).
22
        12. The consideration Plaintiff paid for the policy of home warranty insurance failed.
23

24   That is to say, for the thousands of dollars in premiums paid Defendants, Plaintiff did not

25   receive a dime in compensation. See, California Civil Code 1689 (2)
26
       13. The consideration given became void as a proximate result of the wrongdoing by
27
     Defendants, set forth supra, and in the pleadings and settlement agreements in NJRS and
28   COMPLAINT                                        5
                Case 5:24-cv-04876-VKD Document 1 Filed 08/08/24 Page 6 of 12



1    AZRS. Plaintiff will in due course ask this Court to take judicial notice of the allegations,
2
     findings, and admissions in the settlement agreement of these proceedings pursuant to
3
     Rule 201 of the Federal Rules of Evidence. See, California Civil Code 1689 (3).
4
       14. The consideration for the obligation of Plaintiff to pay premiums failed before it
5

6    was rendered to him. See, California Civil code 1689 (4)

7      15. The public interest will be prejudiced by permitting the contract to stand. Specifically,
8
     contains three adhesive provisions which are void as against public policy:
9
        a. A waiver of attorney’s fees and punitive damages
10
        b. A waiver of a class action remedy and
11

12      c. A purported mandatory mediation and arbitration clause requiring arbitration

13          before the American Arbitration Association.
14
     On May 23rd, 2024, Plaintiff wrote Defendants placing them on notice of the illegality of
15
     these provisions, requesting payment under the policy, and asking for mediation.
16
     Defendants never responded to this letter, though it was sent by Certified Mail and
17

18   receipt of it was acknowledged. So, Defendants waived said mediation and arbitration

19   provision.
20
     The trifecta of these three adhesive provisions is evidence per se of Defendants fraud
21
     malice, and oppression in so far as a consumer, in order to invoke the jurisdiction of the
22
     American Arbitration Association, must pay a $3,125.00 (Three thousand one hundred and
23

24   twenty-five dollar) so-called case initiation fee, which, the evidence will show, is far greater

25   than the average cost of repair/replacement of an appliance under Defendants policies.
26
     So, selection of the American Arbitration Association as the vehicle for a binding arbitration
27
     was intended to defraud Plaintiff – and the Plaintiff class – by disincentivizing victims from
28   COMPLAINT                                         6
                Case 5:24-cv-04876-VKD Document 1 Filed 08/08/24 Page 7 of 12



1    paying out monies in excess of the benefits due to them – and in furtherance of their
2
     pattern and practice or either withholding, or low- balling, benefits payable under the policy. See,
3
     California Civil Code 1689 (6).
4
        16. Plaintiff therefore requests an order rescinding the contract of home insurance and
5

6    restitution of the premium thereunder, individually, and should the class of victims be

7    certified, on their behalf. All such contracts containing the provisions cited supra
8
     are meretricious and void on its face. If Defendants, in view of the foregoing
9
     facts, petition this Court to mandate Arbitration before the American Arbitration Association,
10
     Plaintiff will not only vigorously contest the same but request an award of attorney’s fees
11

12   and costs in so doing.

13                 C.INSURANCE BAD FAITH CALIFORNIA INSURANCE CODE 17200
14
     17. Plaintiff reincorporates and reallege allegations 1 through 16 as though fully set forth herein.
15
     18. The policy of home warranty insurance issued by Defendants on Plaintiff’s Carmel
16
     Valley, California, home are insurance contracts governed by the California Insurance Code
17

18   and regulated by the California Department of Insurance.

19   19. Defendants violated California Insurance Code Section 790.03 (h) 5 and 6 by not attempting,
20
     in good faith, to effectuate prompt, fair, and equitable settlements of claims in which liability has
21
     become reasonably clear, compelling insureds to institute litigation to recover amounts due under
22
     an insurance policy by offering substantially less than the amounts which would ultimately
23

24   recovered in actions brought by the insureds, when the insureds have made claims for amounts

25   reasonably similar to the amounts ultimately recovered. The Defendants are estopped from
26
     denying coverage by the admissions of their own agent that the range in question needed
27

28   COMPLAINT                                         7
                Case 5:24-cv-04876-VKD Document 1 Filed 08/08/24 Page 8 of 12



1    replacement and there is no dispute of fact that the replacement cost exceeded $9,000.00 (Nine
2
     thousand dollars)
3
      20. Defendants are guilty of insurance bad faith, and Plaintiff has, and herewith asserts, a private
4
     right of action pursuant under Business and Professions Code 17200 as mandated by the California
5

6    Supreme Court in Zhang v. Superior Court 178 Cal. App. 4th 14 (2013) for the emotional damages

7    arising from violation of California Insurance Code Section 790.03 (h) 5 and 6. As has been
8
     noted, supra, all of Plaintiff’s interaction with Defendants and/or their so-called adjusters
9
     occurred during the final days of his wife of 60 (sixty) years Susan, who passed away as this
10
     dispute was unfolding, and contributed to and accelerated Plaintiffs emotional pain and suffering.
11

12    21. Plaintiffs have sustained damages as a result of Defendants’ breaches of the policy of

13   homeowner’s warranty insurance including special damages, compensatory damages, attorney’s
14
     fees, and costs, and will ask this Court to award a quantum of punitive damages against
15

16   Defendants to disincentivize them from injuring other prospective customers, prospective

17   insureds. as set forth, supra.
18
              ELDER ABUSE CALIFORNIA WELFARE INSTITUTIONS CODE 15610.30
19
     22. Plaintiff reincorporates and reallege allegations 1 through 21 as though fully set forth herein.
20

21   23. Well aware that many of their targeted customers were elderly and/or on living on retirement

22   funds, and afraid of large bills for replacement of household appliances, Defendants intentionally
23
     willfully. wantonly, and fraudulently intended to accept premiums from such individuals
24
     knowing that they would ‘low-ball’ and/or delay any claims that they might make and made
25
     sure that they signed an agreement waiving their right to damages, or attorney’s fees, or the
26

27   remedy of a class action, and saddling them with an impossible remedy, arbitration of any

28   COMPLAINT                                         8
                Case 5:24-cv-04876-VKD Document 1 Filed 08/08/24 Page 9 of 12



1    disputes before the American Arbitration Association which would typically require a
2
     litigation set up deposit far in excess of the average value of claims made under their policies.
3
     24. California Welfare and Institutions Code 15610. 30 provides as follows:
4
                    (a) “Financial abuse” of an elder or dependent adult occurs when a person or
5

6    entity does any of the following:

7
        (1) Takes, secretes, appropriates, obtains, or retains real or personal property of an elder
8           or dependent adult for a wrongful use or with intent to defraud, or both.

9
     25. Plaintiff is an ‘elder’ under this statute and has suffered ‘financial abuse’ as defined by this
10

11   statute in so far as the premiums paid by Plaintiff are personal property appropriated with an

12   intent to defraud him.
13   25. The members of the prospective class are ‘citizens’ of states which have similar
14
     protections for elders. For example, Nevadans over age 60 (sixty) are protected by
15
     N.R.S. 41.1395 from financial abuse. In Arizona, the Arizona Adult Protective Services
16
     statutes allow civil recovery of an elder’s property -including funds – through a civil suit.
17

18   Plaintiff has carefully refined the class of victims he proposes to represent, for the purposes of

19   this cause of action, to those over 70 who have paid premiums to Defendants without recourse,

20   resident in those states which have special statutes to protect them.
21
     26. These Defendants are guilty of financial abuse of Plaintiff in that their receipt of premiums as
22   contemplated by the California Elder Abuse Statues in so far as their receipt of premiums
23
     without consideration is a wrongful ‘taking’ of his personal property, as evidenced by
24
     their failure to adequately compensate him for his claim, their delay in compensating him
25
     for his claim (they failed to do so entirely) and their attempt to co-opt his remedies against
26

27   him by requiring him to sign an adhesive contract containing a trifecta (as noted supra)

28   COMPLAINT                                         9
               Case 5:24-cv-04876-VKD Document 1 Filed 08/08/24 Page 10 of 12



1    of waivers that are against public policy and therefore null and void.
2
     27. As a direct and proximate result of these Defendants’ violation of California Elder Abuse
3
     Statutes, Plaintiff sustained recoverable damages as provided by law.
4
     28. As a direct and proximate result of these Defendants’ violation of California’s Elder
5

6    Abuse Statutes, Plaintiff is entitled to an award of attorney’s fees and costs.

7    29. These Defendants’ policies, acts, and omissions set forth in the foregoing 28 allegations,
8    are ‘unfair business practices’ within the contemplation of California Civil Code § 3345 and
9
     Plaintiff therefore requests that any damages and attorney’s fees awarded pursuant to California
10
     Elder Abuse Statutes be trebled.
11

12                             E. DECLARATORY RELIEF 28 U.S.C. 2201

13   30. Plaintiff reincorporates and reallege allegations 1 through 29 as though fully set forth herein.
14   31. There is an actual controversy between Plaintiff and Defendants as to the force, effect,
15
     validity of the homeowner’s warranty policy issued by Defendants to Plaintiff.
16
     32. Plaintiff requests that this Court adjudicate the validity of said contract, specifically,
17

18   the validity of the trifecta of waivers contained therein. And, pursuant to Federal Rule of

19   Civil Procedure 57, Plaintiff requests that such adjudication be a speedy one.
20

21
     Wherefore, Plaintiff Prays:
22
         1. That the class hereinbefore defined be certified pursuant to Federal Rule of
23

24   Civil Procedure 23.

25       2. That Plaintiff and the putative class be awarded his and their special damages
26       3. That Plaintiff and the putative class be awarded his and their compensatory damages
27
         4. That Plaintiff and the putative class be awarded damages by way of punishment
28   COMPLAINT                                         10
               Case 5:24-cv-04876-VKD Document 1 Filed 08/08/24 Page 11 of 12



1           and example under the various theories set for supra.
2
         5. That Plaintiff and the putative class be awarded their attorneys’ fees, and that such
3
            attorney’s fees be enhanced by virtue of the benefit this action confers on the class
4
            of elderly folk prayed on by Defendants
5

6        6. That Plaintiff be awarded adequate compensation for representing the class.

7        7. That Plaintiff be awarded his costs of suit.
8
         8. That this case be tried by a jury
9
         9. That this court issue a declaratory judgment declaring the homeowner’s warranty
10
            contract between Plaintiff and Defendants null and void as against public policy.
11

12       10. That Plaintiff be granted such other and further relief as the Court deems

13          appropriate.
14
